verses.zh: 雅各起行，到了东方人之地，
verses.en: So Jacob moved on[NOTE:1] and came to the land of the eastern people.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and Jacob lifted up his feet.” This unusual expression suggests that Jacob had a new lease on life now that God had promised him the blessing he had so desperately tried to gain by his own efforts. The text portrays him as having a new step in his walk.
Heb “the land of the sons of the east.”
verses.commentary:
29:1 "Then Jacob went on his journey" This phrase is translated literally "lifted up his feet"
(VERB, BDB 669, KB 724 and NOUN, BDB 919). This is the only place that this
unique idiom occurs in the OT. It seems to show something of the excitement and purpose that Jacob felt
after his meeting with God at Bethel.

▣ "and came to the land of the sons of the east" In Judges 6:3 and 33 this seems to refer to an
Arabian tribe (cf. Job 1:3; Isa. 11:14; Ezek. 25:4,10). However, here it seems to refer to the inhabitants
of Haran (cf. Jer. 49:28). Possibly, it refers to the northern Arabian tribes between Bethel and Haran that
Jacob might encounter.

verses.zh: 看见田间有一口井，有三群羊卧在井旁；因为人饮羊群都是用那井里的水。井口上的石头是大的。
verses.en: He saw[NOTE:1] in the field a well with[NOTE:2] three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks were watered from that well. Now[NOTE:3] a large stone covered the mouth of the well.
notes: Heb “and he saw, and look.” As in Gen 28:12-15, the narrator uses the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”) here and in the next clause to draw the reader into the story.
Heb “and look, there.”
The disjunctive clause (introduced by the noun with the prefixed conjunction) provides supplemental information that is important to the story.
verses.commentary:
29:2 "He looked, and saw a well in the field" The journey is completely omitted and in Gen. 29:2 Jacob
finds himself close to Haran, but not certain of his exact location. Wells were the place to meet the local
folk. The presence of God is obvious in this "by chance" encounter. Haran is the context for chapters 29-31.

▣ "Now the stone on the mouth of the well was large" This was common in this culture and was

- to stop evaporation

- to keep the water clean

- for the purpose of security (unauthorized use)

- possibly to camouflage its location

- to keep animals from falling into it

verses.zh: 常有羊群在那里聚集，牧人把石头转离井口饮羊，随后又把石头放在井口的原处。
verses.en: When all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds[NOTE:1] would roll the stone off the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would put the stone back in its place over the well’s mouth.
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (the shepherds) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 雅各对牧人说：「弟兄们，你们是哪里来的？」他们说：「我们是哈兰来的。」
verses.en: Jacob asked them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They replied, “We’re from Haran.”
verses.commentary:
29:4 "brothers" This is the use of the term (BDB 26) for a greeting without implying a family
relationship. We use this same greeting among fellow Christians in the southern USA today.

In Gen. 29:12 and 15 the same term is used of a relative, but again not literally a "brother."
This recognition of family is called "my bone and my flesh" in Gen. 29:14 (cf. Gen. 2:23).

verses.zh: 他问他们说：「拿鹤的孙子拉班，你们认识吗？」他们说：「我们认识。」
verses.en: So he said to them, “Do you know Laban, the grandson[NOTE:1] of Nahor?” “We know him,”[NOTE:2] they said.
notes: Heb “son.”

Heb “and they said, ‘We know.’” The word “him” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. In the translation several introductory clauses throughout this section have been placed after the direct discourse they introduce for stylistic reasons as well.
verses.commentary:
29:5 "Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor" Here is a good example where the word "son" (BDB 119) in
Hebrew can refer to "father" or "grandfather." Bethuel is Laban's father and Nahor is his grandfather
(cf. Gen. 24:24,29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ." (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

verses.zh: 雅各说：「他平安吗？」他们说：「平安。看哪，他女儿拉结领着羊来了。」
verses.en: “Is he well?”[NOTE:1] Jacob asked. They replied, “He is well.[NOTE:2] Now look, here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep.”
notes: Heb “and he said to them, ‘Is there peace to him?’”
Heb “peace.”
verses.commentary:
29:6 "Is it well with him. . .It is well" This is the term shalom (BDB 1022).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)

▣ "Rachel his daughter coming with the sheep" There are no coincidences in the lives of God's
servants (cf. Gen. 24:15; Exod. 2:16, see The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life by Hannah Whithall
Smith). There is the unseen hand of God here, as with Joseph in Gen. 37:15-17 (also in the book of Esther
where God's name never appears but His presence and guidance are obvious).

verses.zh: 雅各说：「日头还高，不是羊群聚集的时候，你们不如饮羊，再去放一放。」
verses.en: Then Jacob[NOTE:1] said, “Since it is still the middle of the day,[NOTE:2] it is not time for the flocks to be gathered. You should water the sheep and then go and let them graze some more.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “the day is great.”

Heb “water the sheep and go and pasture [them].” The verbal forms are imperatives, but Jacob would hardly be giving direct orders to someone else’s shepherds. The nuance here is probably one of advice.
verses.commentary:
29:7 "Behold, it was still high day" Jacob was a shepherd and he knew that what was being done was
against the best shepherding practices (this knowledge will impress Laban). This will allow him to show
off his muscles (cf. Gen. 29:10) for Rachel! Apparently, it worked! I bet Rachel was shocked at being
kissed by this stranger (cf. Gen. 29:11), but after he told her who he was there was great joy. The fact
that Jacob weeps shows the cultural propensity of Oriental men to show their emotions much more than their
western counterparts (cf. Gen. 29:13).

Jacob addresses the other shepherds in idiomatic IMPERATIVES functioning as
rhetorical questions.

- water, BDB 1052, KB 1639, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- go, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE

- pasture, BDB 944, KB 1258, Qal IMPERATIVE

verses.zh: 他们说：「我们不能，必等羊群聚齐，人把石头转离井口才可饮羊。」
verses.en: “We can’t,” they said, “until all the flocks are gathered and the stone is rolled off the mouth of the well. Then we water[NOTE:1] the sheep.”
notes: The perfect verbal forms with the vav (ו) consecutive carry on the sequence begun by the initial imperfect form.

verses.zh: 雅各正和他们说话的时候，拉结领着她父亲的羊来了，因为那些羊是她牧放的。
verses.en: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep, for she was tending them.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “was a shepherdess.”

verses.zh: 雅各看见母舅拉班的女儿拉结和母舅拉班的羊群，就上前把石头转离井口，饮他母舅拉班的羊群。
verses.en: When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his uncle Laban,[NOTE:1] and the sheep of his uncle Laban, he[NOTE:2] went over[NOTE:3] and rolled the stone off the mouth of the well and watered the sheep of his uncle Laban.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Laban, the brother of his mother” (twice in this verse).
Heb “Jacob.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “drew near, approached.”

Heb “Laban, the brother of his mother.” The text says nothing initially about the beauty of Rachel. But the reader is struck by the repetition of “Laban the brother of his mother.” G. J. Wenham is no doubt correct when he observes that Jacob’s primary motive at this stage is to ingratiate himself with Laban (Genesis [WBC], 2:231).

verses.zh: 雅各与拉结亲嘴，就放声而哭。
verses.en: Then Jacob kissed Rachel and began to weep loudly.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and he lifted up his voice and wept.” The idiom calls deliberate attention to the fact that Jacob wept out loud.

verses.zh: 雅各告诉拉结，自己是她父亲的外甥，是利百加的儿子，拉结就跑去告诉她父亲。
verses.en: When Jacob explained[NOTE:1] to Rachel that he was a relative of her father[NOTE:2] and the son of Rebekah, she ran and told her father.
notes: Heb “declared.”
Heb “that he [was] the brother of her father.”

verses.zh: 拉班听见外甥雅各的信息，就跑去迎接，抱着他，与他亲嘴，领他到自己的家。雅各将一切的情由告诉拉班。
verses.en: When Laban heard this news about Jacob, his sister’s son, he rushed out to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob[NOTE:1] told Laban how he was related to him.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “and he told to Laban all these things.” This might mean Jacob told Laban how he happened to be there, but Laban’s response (see v. 14) suggests “all these things” refers to what Jacob had previously told Rachel (see v. 12).
verses.commentary:
29:13 "when Laban heard the news of Jacob his sister's son, he ran to meet him" The rabbis say he ran
because he thought that Jacob would have presents just as Eliezer had brought (Gen. 24:10). However, I'm not
ready to impugn his motives at this point. It is true that Laban is going to out-manipulate Jacob, the
manipulator, but this seems to be the plan of God for maturing Jacob.

verses.zh: 拉班对他说：「你实在是我的骨肉。」雅各就和他同住了一个月。
verses.en: Then Laban said to him, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.”[NOTE:1] So Jacob[NOTE:2] stayed with him for a month.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “indeed, my bone and my flesh are you.” The expression sounds warm enough, but the presence of “indeed” may suggest that Laban had to be convinced of Jacob’s identity before permitting him to stay. To be one’s “bone and flesh” is to be someone’s blood relative. For example, the phrase describes the relationship between Abimelech and the Shechemites (Judg 9:2; his mother was a Shechemite); David and the Israelites (2 Sam 5:1); David and the elders of Judah (2 Sam 19:12); and David and his nephew Amasa (2 Sam 19:13; see 2 Sam 17:2; 1 Chr 2:16-17).
Heb “and he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “a month of days.”
verses.commentary:
29:14 "a month" The term (BDB 294) is related to the term "moon" (BDB 294). The Hebrews used a lunar
calendar marked by the phases of the moon (i.e., new moon, new month).

verses.zh: 拉班对雅各说：「你虽是我的骨肉（原文是弟兄），岂可白白地服事我？请告诉我，你要甚么为工价？」
verses.en: Then Laban said to Jacob, “Should you work[NOTE:1] for me for nothing because you are my relative?[NOTE:2] Tell me what your wages should be.”
notes: The verb is the perfect with the vav (ו) consecutive; the nuance in the question is deliberative.
Heb “my brother.” The term “brother” is used in a loose sense; actually Jacob was Laban’s nephew.
verses.commentary:
29:15 This is very subtle, but it seems that Laban had already caught on to the idea that Jacob had
an eye for Rachel and he was in a round-about way asserting that since Jacob did not have the dowry he could
work for him. Possibly he had also noted his shepherding skills.

verses.zh: 拉班有两个女儿，大的名叫利亚，小的名叫拉结。
verses.en: (Now Laban had two daughters;[NOTE:1] the older one was named Leah, and the younger one Rachel.
notes: Heb “and to Laban [there were] two daughters.” The disjunctive clause (introduced here by a conjunction and a prepositional phrase) provides supplemental material that is important to the story. Since this material is parenthetical in nature, vv. 16-17 have been set in parentheses in the translation.
verses.commentary:
29:16 "Leah" The etymology of her name (BDB 521, KB 513) is somewhat in dispute:

- Akkadian root, "cow"

- Arabic root, "wild cow"

- "wearied" (from VERB, KB 512).

From Gen. 29:17 it seems that she was not as attractive physically as was Rachel.

▣ "Rachel" Her name meant "a ewe" (BDB 932, KB 1216). Apparently, nomadic people were often
named after animals.

verses.zh: 利亚的眼睛没有神气，拉结却生得美貌俊秀。
verses.en: Leah’s eyes were tender,[NOTE:1] but Rachel had a lovely figure and beautiful appearance.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and the eyes of Leah were tender.” The disjunctive clause (introduced here by a conjunction and a noun) continues the parenthesis begun in v. 16. It is not clear what is meant by “tender” (or “delicate”) eyes. The expression may mean she had appealing eyes (cf. NAB, NRSV, NLT), though some suggest that they were plain, not having the brightness normally expected. Either way, she did not measure up to her gorgeous sister.
Heb “and Rachel was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.”
verses.commentary:
29:17

NASB, RSV, JPSOA, NIV, LXX
"eyes were weak"

NKJV
"eyes were delicate"

NRSV
"eyes were lovely"

TEV, NJB
"lovely eyes"

REB
"dull eyes"

Peshitta
"attractive eyes"

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 940, KB 1230) means

- Hebrew root ‒ soft, tender, slender

- Arabic root ‒ weak, thin, poor

Most English translations choose the Arabic connotation in this context because of the root meaning
of her name. But, this verse may be an attempt to compliment both girls. In countries where women wear veils,
the eyes are all that can be seen and, therefore, are very important.

▣ "beautiful of form and face" The ADJECTIVE (BDB 421) is used twice in two
CONSTRUCTS.

- BDB 421 and BDB 1061 denote fair/beautiful in form

- BDB 421 and BDB 909 denote fair/beautiful in appearance

All of the primary Patriarchs' wives were beautiful, attractive (but barren) women.

verses.zh: 雅各爱拉结，就说：「我愿为你小女儿拉结服事你七年。」
verses.en: Since Jacob had fallen in love with[NOTE:1] Rachel, he said, “I’ll serve you seven years in exchange for your younger daughter Rachel.”
notes: Heb “Jacob loved.”
verses.commentary:
29:18 "Now Jacob loved Rachel. . .and I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel"
This was a very generous offer, far more than Laban would ever have asked. But he was thrilled and took
full advantage of it. Something of the true love between these two can be seen in Gen. 29:19-20,30.

verses.zh: 拉班说：「我把她给你，胜似给别人，你与我同住吧！」
verses.en: Laban replied, “I’d rather give her to you than to another man.[NOTE:1] Stay with me.”
notes: Heb “Better my giving her to you than my giving her to another man.”
verses.commentary:
29:19 "stay with me" This is a command (BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE), but in
context it is an idiomatic way of accepting Jacob's offer to work seven years for Laban as a price for
a bride.

verses.zh: 雅各就为拉结服事了七年；他因为深爱拉结，就看这七年如同几天。
verses.en: So Jacob worked for seven years to acquire Rachel.[NOTE:1] But they seemed like only a few days to him[NOTE:2] because his love for her was so great.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “in exchange for Rachel.”

But they seemed like only a few days to him. This need not mean that the time passed quickly. More likely it means that the price seemed insignificant when compared to what he was getting in the bargain.
Heb “because of his love for her.” The words “was so great” are supplied for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 雅各对拉班说：「日期已经满了，求你把我的妻子给我，我好与她同房。」
verses.en: Finally Jacob said[NOTE:1] to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my time of service is up.[NOTE:2] And I want to sleep with her.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and Jacob said.”
Heb “my days are fulfilled.”

Heb “I want to approach.” The verb בּוֹא (boʾ) with the preposition אֶל (ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations. The verb is a cohortative; it may be subordinated to the preceding request, “so that I may sleep with,” or it may be an independent clause expressing his desire.
verses.commentary:
29:21 "Then Jacob said to Laban, 'Give me my wife, for my time is completed, that I may go in
to her'" Obviously, Laban was in no hurry even at the end of seven years, to give Jacob his daughter.
This shows something of the tendency that will be seen throughout these verses concerning the manipulative
techniques of Laban. He was looking out for his immediate family's interests.

verses.zh: 拉班就摆设筵席，请齐了那地方的众人。
verses.en: So Laban invited all the people[NOTE:1] of that place and prepared a feast.
notes: Heb “men.”

verses.zh: 到晚上，拉班将女儿利亚送来给雅各，雅各就与她同房。
verses.en: In the evening he brought his daughter Leah[NOTE:1] to Jacob,[NOTE:2] and he slept with her.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and it happened in the evening that he took Leah his daughter and brought her.”sn His daughter Leah. Laban’s deception of Jacob by giving him the older daughter instead of the younger was God’s way of disciplining the deceiver who tricked his older brother. D. Kidner says this account is “the very embodiment of anti-climax, and this moment a miniature of man’s disillusion, experienced from Eden onwards” (Genesis [TOTC], 160). G. von Rad notes, “That Laban secretly gave the unloved Leah to the man in love was, to be sure, a monstrous blow, a masterpiece of shameless treachery…It was certainly a move by which he won for himself far and wide the coarsest laughter” (Genesis [OTL], 291).
Heb “to him”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “came to” or “approached,” a euphemism for sexual relations. See note at v. 21.
verses.commentary:
29:23 "Jacob went in to her" There has been much discussion about why Jacob, after all this
time, did not know that this was Leah. Some of the theories are:

- it was dark (i.e., Gen. 29:23, "in the evening")

- she was veiled (cf. Gen. 24:65)

- he was drunk (the term "feast" [BDB 1059] in Gen. 29:22 is from the root "to drink" [BDB 1059],
implying a wild party)!

It seems to me that #3 fits the social context the best.

There are several VERBS which denote sexual activity.

- lie with, BDB 1011, KB 1486, cf. Gen. 19:32; 26:10; 30:15; 39:7; Lev. 18:22

- approach, BDB 897, KB 1132, cf. Gen. 20:4; Lev. 18:6,14,19; 20:16

- go in to, BDB 97, KB 112, cf. Gen. 19:31; 29:21,23,30; 30:3,4,16; 38:8,9,16; 39:14

- know, BDB 393, KB 390, cf. Gen. 4:1,17,25; 19:5,8; 24:16; 38:26; Num. 31:17,18,35;
Jdgs. 19:22,25; 21:12

verses.zh: 拉班又将婢女悉帕给女儿利亚作使女。
verses.en: (Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.)[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and Laban gave to her Zilpah his female servant, to Leah his daughter [for] a servant.” This clause gives information parenthetical to the narrative.
verses.commentary:
29:24 "Laban also gave his maid Zilpah to his daughter Leah as a maid" We learn from the Nuzi Tablets,
which describe the Hurrian culture of the same period (2nd millennium B.C.), that
this was a common practice. In case the daughter was barren, the servant could bear a child in her behalf
(cf. Gen. 29:28-29; 30:3). Verses 24 and 29 are a narrator's parenthesis preparing us for chapter 30.

verses.zh: 到了早晨，雅各一看是利亚，就对拉班说：「你向我做的是甚么事呢？我服事你，不是为拉结吗？你为甚么欺哄我呢？」
verses.en: In the morning Jacob discovered it was Leah![NOTE:1] So Jacob[NOTE:2] said to Laban, “What in the world have you done to me?[NOTE:3] Didn’t I work for you in exchange for Rachel? Why have you tricked[NOTE:4] me?”
notes: Heb “and it happened in the morning that look, it was Leah.” By the use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), the narrator invites the reader to view the scene through Jacob’s eyes.
Heb “and he said”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb What is this you have done to me?” The use of the pronoun “this” is enclitic, adding emphasis to the question: “What in the world have you done to me?”

The Hebrew verb translated tricked here (רָמָה, ramah) is cognate to the noun used in Gen 27:35 to describe Jacob’s deception of Esau. Jacob is discovering that what goes around, comes around. See J. A. Diamond, “The Deception of Jacob: A New Perspective on an Ancient Solution to the Problem,” VT 34 (1984): 211-13.
verses.commentary:
29:25 "behold, it was Leah" Although it was obvious from Laban's character that this kind of behavior
was to be expected, it is surprising that Leah did not say something or that Rachel did not say something.
But, we must judge this day in light of its own culture and not in ours, and because of the lack of specific
textual information modern interpreters must not speculate.

verses.zh: 拉班说：「大女儿还没有给人，先把小女儿给人，在我们这地方没有这规矩。
verses.en: “It is not our custom here,”[NOTE:1] Laban replied, “to give the younger daughter in marriage[NOTE:2] before the firstborn.
notes: Heb “and Laban said, ‘It is not done so in our place.’” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “to give the younger.” The words “daughter” and “in marriage” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 你为这个满了七日，我就把那个也给你，你再为她服事我七年。」
verses.en: Complete my older daughter’s bridal week.[NOTE:1] Then we will give you the younger one[NOTE:2] too, in exchange for seven more years of work.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Bridal week. An ancient Hebrew marriage ceremony included an entire week of festivities (cf. Judg 14:12).tn Heb “fulfill the period of seven of this one.” The referent of “this one” has been specified in the translation as “my older daughter” for clarity.
Heb “this other one.”

Heb “and we will give to you also this one in exchange for labor which you will work with me, still seven other years.”sn In exchange for seven more years of work. See C. H. Gordon, “The Story of Jacob and Laban in the Light of the Nuzi Tablets,” BASOR 66 (1937): 25-27; and J. Van Seters, “Jacob’s Marriages and Ancient Near Eastern Customs: A Reassessment,” HTR 62 (1969): 377-95.
verses.commentary:
29:27 "complete the bridal week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service
which you shall serve with me for another seven years" This bridal week was common to this culture
(cf. Jdg. 14:12,17). It is also reflected in the extra-canonical book of Tobit 11:18. The concept of
the month being broken into weeks is uniquely biblical (cf. Gen. 2:1, 2). The fact that Laban could
make the unbelievable request that Jacob serve him seven more years shows the exploitive attitude of
this man. Jacob has met his match and now knows how it feels to be tricked (cf. Gen. 27:35).

verses.zh: 雅各就如此行。满了利亚的七日，拉班便将女儿拉结给雅各为妻。
verses.en: Jacob did as Laban said.[NOTE:1] When Jacob[NOTE:2] completed Leah’s bridal week,[NOTE:3] Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and Jacob did so.” The words “as Laban said” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “the seven of this one.” The referent of “this one” has been specified in the translation as Leah to avoid confusion with Rachel, mentioned later in the verse.
Heb “and he gave to him Rachel his daughter for him for a wife.” The referent of the pronoun “he” (Laban) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 拉班又将婢女辟拉给女儿拉结作使女。
verses.en: (Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.)[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah his female servant, for her for a servant.”

verses.zh: 雅各也与拉结同房，并且爱拉结胜似爱利亚，于是又服事了拉班七年。
verses.en: Jacob[NOTE:1] slept with[NOTE:2] Rachel as well. He also loved Rachel more than Leah. Then he worked for Laban[NOTE:3] for seven more years.
notes: Heb “and he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “came to” or “approached,” a euphemism for sexual relations. See note at v. 21.
Heb “him”; the referent (Laban) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 耶和华见利亚失宠（原文是被恨；下同），就使她生育，拉结却不生育。
verses.en: When the Lord saw that Leah was unloved,[NOTE:1] he enabled her to become pregnant[NOTE:2] while Rachel remained childless.
notes: Heb “hated.” The rhetorical device of overstatement is used (note v. 30, which says simply that Jacob loved Rachel more than he did Leah) to emphasize that Rachel, as Jacob’s true love and the primary object of his affections, had an advantage over Leah.
Heb “he opened up her womb.”
verses.commentary:
29:31 "unloved" This is a Hebrew idiom which is, literally, "hated" (BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal
PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Gen. 29:33), but because of its use in Deut. 21:15; Mal. 1:2-3;
John 12:25 and Luke 14:26, we know that it is simply an idiom of comparison which should be translated
"unloved," not "hated." It speaks of priority. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.

verses.zh: 利亚怀孕生子，就给他起名叫流便（就是有儿子的意思），因而说：「耶和华看见我的苦情，如今我的丈夫必爱我。」
verses.en: So Leah became pregnant[NOTE:1] and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben,[NOTE:2] for she said, “The Lord has looked with pity on my oppressed condition.[NOTE:3] Surely my husband will love me now.”
notes: Or “Leah conceived” (also in vv. 33, 34, 35).
The name Reuben (רְאוּבֵן, reʾuven) means “look, a son.”

Leah’s explanation of the name Reuben reflects a popular etymology, not an exact one. The name means literally “look, a son.” Playing on the Hebrew verb “look,” she observes that the Lord has “looked” with pity on her oppressed condition. See further S. R. Driver, Genesis, 273. tn Heb “looked on my affliction.”
verses.commentary:
29:32 "Leah conceived and bore him a son and named him Reuben" Reuben (BDB 910, "behold a son" from
the VERB "to see," BDB 909) is the popular etymology for the term "seen" (BDB 906, KB 1157,
Qal PERFECT, "to see").

▣ To bear a son was a great honor. Leah was certain Jacob would be pleased and acknowledge
her with more attention.

verses.zh: 她又怀孕生子，就说：「耶和华因为听见我失宠，所以又赐给我这个儿子」，于是给他起名叫西缅（就是听见的意思）。
verses.en: She became pregnant again and had another son. She said, “Because the Lord heard that I was unloved,[NOTE:1] he gave me this one too.” So she named him Simeon.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “hated.” See the note on the word “unloved” in v. 31.

The name Simeon (שִׁמְעוֹן, shimʿon) is derived from the verbal root שָׁמַע (shamaʿ) and means “hearing.” The name is appropriate since it is reminder that the Lord “heard” about Leah’s unloved condition and responded with pity.
verses.commentary:
29:33 "Then she conceived again and bore a son. . .Simeon" The word "Simeon" (BDB 1035) is the popular
etymology from the Hebrew word "heard" or "the Lord heard" (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal
PERFECT).

verses.zh: 她又怀孕生子，起名叫利未（就是联合的意思），说：「我给丈夫生了三个儿子，他必与我联合。」
verses.en: She became pregnant again and had another son. She said, “Now this time my husband will show me affection,[NOTE:1] because I have given birth to three sons for him.” That is why he was named Levi.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “will be joined to me.”
The name Levi (לֵוִי, levi), the precise meaning of which is debated, was appropriate because it sounds like the verb לָוָה (lavah, “to join”), used in the statement recorded earlier in the verse.
verses.commentary:
29:34 "She conceived again and bore a son. . .Levi" His name (BDB 532 I) is from the popular etymology
for "joined" (BDB 530 I, KB 522, Niphal IMPERFECT). Leah longed for a deeper emotional
relationship with Jacob.

verses.zh: 她又怀孕生子，说：「这回我要赞美耶和华」，因此给他起名叫犹大（就是赞美的意思）。这才停了生育。
verses.en: She became pregnant again and had another son. She said, “This time I will praise the Lord.” That is why she named him Judah.[NOTE:1] Then she stopped having children.
notes: The name Judah (יְהוּדָה, yehudah) means “he will be praised” and reflects the sentiment Leah expresses in the statement recorded earlier in the verse. For further discussion see W. F. Albright, “The Names ‘Israel’ and ‘Judah’ with an Excursus on the Etymology of Todah and Torah,” JBL 46 (1927): 151-85; and A. R. Millard, “The Meaning of the Name Judah,” ZAW 86 (1974): 216-18.
verses.commentary:
29:35 "she conceived again and bore a son. . .Judah" This one is the son that God chose to fulfill His
promise. His name means "praise" (BDB 397), which is a play on "I will praise YHWH" (BDB 392, KB 389,
Hiphil IMPERFECT). His name becomes the name of a tribe, then a nation, and then all
Jewish people. The three older sons will be rejected because of their improper acts. Again, it is interesting
that God chose the woman who was less loved to bring forth the line of the Messiah. This reversal of expected
events is common in Genesis and shows YHWH's control and sovereignty.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: GENESIS 29:1-3

1Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the sons of the east. 2He looked, and saw a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep were lying there beside it, for from that well they watered the flocks. Now the stone on the mouth of the well was large. 3When all the flocks were gathered there, they would then roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place on the mouth of the well.
